newsitem.title: FRANCE: Ad expert Carat fuels French TV audience debate.
newsitem.headline: Ad expert Carat fuels French TV audience debate.

text.p: Carat Expert, the measurement arm of French advertising space specialist Carat, said on Tuesday there had been a serious slide in the number of people watching television in France in the first part of this year.
Last week French audience measurement body Mediametrie denied newspaper reports that the French TV audience had shrivelled in the first quarter.

"Following numerous commentaries on the figures for change in the television audience, Carat confirms that there is in fact a significant and exceptional fall in the television audience, as has been noted in all the media agencies," Carat Expert said in a statement.
It said the fall was seen in both the length of time spent watching and in the number of viewers.
"This (fall) comes to at least 1.3 million viewers over the period from February 3, 1997 to April 20, 1997 compared with the same period of 1996," Carat Expert's statement said.
It said the difference between its figures and other published figures was due to differences in calculation methods.
Carat said it only counts as viewers people who switch on their television set for at least a minute.

"The level of a second is not judged sufficiently reliable because it automatically includes people who turn on their television to use it for other things, such as for computer games," Carat Expert said.
It said its method of calculating audience numbers had been used and recognised by the advertising profession for several years.
Mediametrie last week published figures showing that more people in France watched television at least once a day in the first quarter of 1997 than the same period a year earlier.
"It is therefore difficult to say that a million television viewers have disappeared, as has unfortunately been asserted," Mediametrie said at the time.
There had been a fall of four minutes in the length of time viewers spent in front of their televisions in the first quarter, Mediametrie said.

Unseasonable weather was the main reason for the changes, with unusually fine weather in February and March, Mediametrie said. The same viewing variations had been noted in neighbouring European countries, it added.
Carat seemed sceptical of Mediametrie's explanation, although its statement did not mention Mediametrie by name.

"If the fall is in fact linked to the exceptional weather of these last few months, it probably also reveals the existence of new expectations on the part of television viewers," Carat Expert's statement said.
It did not explain what new expectations to which it was referring. No one was immediately available at Carat to comment.
